beats.intro: Alternative investments, module one. [[sub]]What makes an investment alternative, the three ways to invest in one, and how managers are paid.
beats.what: [[a]]Alternative investments are everything other than public equity, public fixed income, and cash. They are grouped together not because they resemble one another, but because they differ from traditional assets. [[f1]]They call for specialized knowledge to value their cash flows and risks. [[f2]]Their returns typically have low correlation with traditional assets. [[f3]]They are illiquid, with long time horizons and large capital outlays. [[res]]Those features lead to special investment structures, incentive-based fees to reduce information gaps between managers and investors, and challenges in appraising performance. [[who]]Investors with the longest horizons, such as pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and endowments, hold the most.
beats.cats: [[a]]There are three categories. [[pc]]Private capital is funding for companies that comes from neither public equity nor public debt markets. As equity, it is private equity. As loans, it is private debt. [[ra]]Real assets are generally tangible: real estate, infrastructure, natural resources such as farmland, timberland and commodities, plus collectibles and intangibles like patents. Digital assets are a newer addition. [[hf]]Hedge funds are private vehicles distinguished by how they invest, not what they hold. They use leverage, derivatives, and short selling.
beats.life: [[a]]Private capital serves companies at different stages of life. [[vc]]Venture capital is private equity for the startup phase: small companies with big growth potential, like an early-stage digital media firm. Venture debt lends to early-stage firms with little cash flow. [[pe]]Private equity proper is mostly used for mature companies, or those in decline. A manager might restructure a struggling manufacturer, sell business lines, upgrade its plant, and either sell the company or take it public again several years later. Leveraged buyouts are a key approach. [[dd]]Distressed debt targets issuers near bankruptcy, where investors with restructuring skills can benefit.
beats.methods: [[a]]There are three ways in. [[fund]]Fund investing: the investor contributes capital, and the fund selects and manages the investments. It is the usual starting point, with little control, and a management fee plus a performance fee. [[co]]Co-investing: the investor is in the fund, and also has the right to invest directly alongside it in a specific deal, at lower fees. It builds experience. [[ex]]For instance, a fund wants to buy a company for one and a half billion dollars, but may invest at most one billion in any one deal. It offers the other half billion to its investors as a co-investment, with reduced fees and no performance fee. [[dir]]Direct investing: no intermediary at all. Maximum control over selection, financing and timing, but it demands specialized skills and resources. Only the largest investors do it.
beats.lp: [[a]]Most alternative funds are limited partnerships. [[gp]]The general partner manages the fund, and has theoretically unlimited liability. [[lp]]The limited partners are the outside investors. They are passive, and their liability is capped at what they invest. They usually commit to put in capital over time, so the upfront cash outflow can be a fraction of the commitment. [[lpa]]A limited partnership agreement sets the terms: profit sharing, roles, and the rules on transfers and dissolution. [[side]]A side letter can modify terms for one investor. A most favored nation clause ensures any better terms granted to other investors also apply to that investor.
beats.other: [[a]]Other assets use other structures. [[ppp]]Infrastructure often uses a public-private partnership. A special purpose entity raises debt and equity to build and run a project, under a concession agreement giving exclusive operating rights for a fixed period. In Indonesia, for example, a plan to spend one hundred fifty billion dollars would be funded thirty percent by government, and seventy percent by private investors. [[liq]]More liquid vehicles exist as well: master limited partnerships, real estate investment trusts, commodity funds, and exchange-traded funds.
beats.fees: [[a]]Alternative managers earn a management fee, often one to two percent, plus a performance fee. [[commit]]Private equity charges the management fee on committed capital, not invested capital. That removes the incentive to deploy money quickly just to raise fees. Hedge funds charge on assets under management. [[hurdle]]The performance fee usually applies only above a hurdle rate, also called the preferred return. With a hard hurdle, the manager takes a share only of returns above the hurdle. [[ex]]A fund earns eighteen percent. The hurdle is eight, and the performance fee is twenty percent of the excess. The manager earns twenty percent of ten, which is two percent. The investors keep sixteen. [[cu]]A catch-up clause speeds things up. Investors get everything up to eight percent. Then the manager receives distributions until it holds twenty percent of all profit: two percent more. The remaining eight is split eighty-twenty. The manager's total rises to three point six percent, and investors keep fourteen point four.
beats.protect: [[a]]Other terms protect investors. [[hwm]]A high-water mark, common in hedge funds, means no performance fee is charged until the fund recovers past its previous peak value, so investors do not pay twice for the same gains. [[claw]]A clawback lets investors reclaim performance fees paid earlier, if later deals lose money. [[wf]]Waterfalls set the order of distributions. In a deal-by-deal, or American, waterfall, the manager is paid fees as each deal is sold, even before investors have recovered their capital and hurdle across the whole fund. In a whole-of-fund, or European, waterfall, investors receive everything until they have their capital and hurdle back, and only then does the manager share in profit. [[cb]]In one example, a manager is paid two, three and eight million dollars on three early wins. Later deals break even or lose, and the fund as a whole breaks even. A clawback requires the manager to return all thirteen million.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Alternatives differ from traditional assets: illiquid, long-term, specialized, and often lowly correlated. [[w2]]The categories are private capital, real assets, and hedge funds. [[w3]]Investors can go through a fund, alongside it, or directly, with more control and lower fees as they move toward direct. [[w4]]Limited partnerships align manager and investor with management and performance fees, hurdles, high-water marks, clawbacks and waterfalls.
beats.finish: Module one of alternative investments is complete. Next: performance and returns.
